site.name: Positive
site.intro: Five small retellings from India’s living story traditions. Read one, then return to your day a little lighter.

stories.title: Krishna's Gentle Mission to Hastinapura
stories.source: Mahabharata — Udyoga Parva (Van Buitenen translation, Wikipedia overview)
body: Before the great war, Krishna traveled to Dhritarashtra's court at Hastinapura as a peace envoy for the Pandavas. With calm resolve, he offered the Kauravas a modest beginning: only five villages, or even five small houses joined together, enough to live in dignity and avoid bloodshed.

When the proud Duryodhana rose and tried to bind him there in the assembly, Krishna laughed softly and revealed his radiant divine form. The gathered kings trembled in awe, yet the beloved emissary slipped away unharmed, carrying one last chance for peace across the land.

He returned to the Pandavas with hope still alive, though Dhritarashtra's heart ached with grief at the choice before him. In that tender moment between war and reconciliation, compassion lingered, reminding all that even pride can yield when mercy is offered.

stories.title: The Jackal's Gentle Cleverness
stories.source: Jataka Tales — Ellen C. Babbitt (1912), Project Gutenberg
body: Near a quiet lake, a great elephant king stumbled into a hunter's rope, and his mighty roar rang across the trees. None of the animals nearby could loosen the snare, and his strength alone was not enough to break free.

A small jackal padded up and spoke softly, asking the elephant to close one eye at a time. With each gentle tug, a foot slipped loose from the noose, until at last the great beast stood free upon the ground.

The elephant lowered his long trunk and swore a lasting friendship with the little jackal. From that day forward, the smallest voice and the kindest thought had proven stronger than any rope the hunter could lay.

stories.title: The Honest Son's Golden Reward
stories.source: More Jataka Tales — Ellen C. Babbitt (1922), Project Gutenberg
body: On his deathbed, an old woodcutter pressed his son's hand and whispered of a costly golden axe hidden beneath a tree. He begged the lad to carry it safely to a merchant in the distant capital, trusting that truth would light his way.

The merchant, unaccustomed to plain and honest folk, set a quiet test. He set out three axes on the mat — one bright gold, one shining silver, and a humble iron one. When he asked which lay buried, the boy pointed without hesitation to the iron.

A warm smile softened the merchant's face, for such simple honesty was rare and precious. Delighted, he placed the golden axe, the silver axe, and the iron axe all into the young man's arms, sending him home richly rewarded.

stories.title: Gajendra's Lotus Call to Heaven
body: On the slopes of Mount Trikuta, the elephant-king Gajendra waded into the lake of Tillai for his morning bath, when a crocodile clamped onto his foot and dragged him toward the deep. He struggled and trumpeted through the long hours, strength fading as the water swirled around him.

Exhausted at last, he reached upward with his trunk and lifted a lotus toward the sky, calling softly from his heart to the Lord who dwells in every being. Before his cry had faded, the Lord appeared on a cloud, His discus flashing like dawn.

With a single merciful blow, He freed Gajendra from the crocodile's jaws and touched the devoted elephant, who stood radiant and at peace. Purified by that vision, Gajendra entered the spiritual world and received salokya, a place beside Krishna forever.

stories.title: Krishna Lets His Mother Tie Him
body: Little Krishna had crept into the kitchen again, tipping a yogurt pot and slipping butter to the waiting monkeys with a laugh. By the time Mother Yasoda found the mess, the floor was dotted with tiny footprints and sticky handprints, and she decided the mischief had to stop that very moment.

She fetched a heavy grinding mortar and began tying Him to it, but every rope she tried fell short by two fingers. Neighbours and household women gathered at the doorway, watching in wonder as rope after rope proved too small for the small boy, though no one could say why.

At last Krishna smiled and allowed Himself to be bound, showing that even the Infinite yields to a mother's love. In that quiet surrender lies a gentle hope: no trouble is too small, no heart too vast, to be held by tenderness.
